cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and TRI clones
processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea in broken grades; during the dry season a seasonal dry wind, the cachan, stresses the leaf and concentrates its aromatic compounds, giving the famous pungent 'Uva character'.
harvest_season: Year-round, but the dry season, mainly July and August and sometimes into early September, is the quality window; outside it the teas are plainer.
appearance_dry: Small, tightly twisted dark broken leaf, slightly reddish.
appearance_liquor: Deep orange-red, bright, with a coppery rim.
taste_profile: Pungent and distinctive: a cooling, wintergreen-like aroma over a strong, brisk body with firm tannin and a sweet finish.

brewing.notes: Stands up to a full boil and takes milk well.

vintage_note: Sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade; the 'Uva season' invoices from July and August, sometimes into early September, are the ones to seek out. Buy a current-season lot and drink within a year; tea labelled simply 'Uva' from outside the season will be milder.
description:
Uva is the eastern slope of Sri Lanka's central highlands, around Badulla, Bandarawela and Haputale at roughly 900 to 1,500 metres, and it makes the most distinctive of the Ceylon teas. For a few weeks each year a dry wind, the cachan, sweeps over the hills, stressing the bushes and concentrating the aromatic compounds in the leaf; the teas made in that window have a pungent, almost wintergreen-like character that blenders prize.

Manufacture is orthodox, mostly broken grades (BOP, BOPF), with a wither, rolling, quick oxidation and firing. Outside the dry season the same estates make pleasant but ordinary tea; the 'Uva season', mainly July and August and sometimes into early September, is the whole point.

The cup is deep orange-red and bright, strong and brisk with a cooling, mentholated aroma, firm tannin and a sweet finish. It stands up to a full boil and takes milk well, and blenders value it. Three to four minutes with water off the boil, with or without milk.

It is sold through the weekly Colombo auction by estate and grade, and the invoices from the season, are the ones to seek out. Buy a current-season lot and drink it within a year. Tea labelled simply 'Uva' outside the season will be milder.
sources_note: The trade name for the seasonal dry wind ('Cachan') was left out as unverified; estate names from memory.
history:
Dambatenne, one of Sri Lanka's oldest tea factories, was established in 1890.

What sets the region apart is a seasonal dry wind, known as the cachan, which blows through in the middle of the year and stresses the bushes into producing the volatile compounds behind the Uva character. The seasonal teas come mainly in July and August, sometimes into early September.

The cooling, wintergreen-like character from those weeks made Uva a tea that blenders look for, and teas from this short window remain the region's calling card.
